content: No significant differences in efficacy have been observed among the various Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) conjugate vaccines. However, failure to administer the PRP-OMP vaccine for the initial dose has been linked to an increased incidence of Hib disease in American Indian/Alaska Native (AI/AN) infants residing in communities where Hib transmission remains active and exposure to colonized individuals is likely. Additionally, maintaining stocks of both PRP-OMP and other Hib conjugate vaccine formulations within the same clinical setting may inadvertently result in the administration of a non-PRP-OMP vaccine for the first Hib dose. To mitigate this risk, clinics predominantly serving AI/AN children may choose to stock and exclusively use PRP-OMP-containing Hib vaccines. For combination vaccines such as DTaP-IPV/Hib, distinct lot numbers are assigned to the DTaP-IPV component and the Hib powder component. Healthcare providers are advised to document these lot numbers separately to ensure accurate record-keeping. The Get Smart About Antibiotics Week, observed from October 6–10, 2008, emphasizes the theme The power to prevent resistance is in your hands. The inappropriate use of antibiotics, particularly for treating upper respiratory infections (URIs), poses unnecessary risks of adverse events and contributes to the development of antibiotic resistance. Adverse events associated with antibiotic use, most commonly allergic reactions or drug intolerance, accounted for an estimated 142,500 emergency department visits annually in the United States during 2004–2006. Furthermore, the inappropriate and excessive use of antimicrobials increases the risk of antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections within a community. Such infections can result in severe or prolonged illness, hospitalization, and, in some cases, death.
